claim: Lorente de No suggested that reverberatory activity sequences in small networks could sustain activity.
source: Lorente de No suggested that reverberatory activity sequences in small networks could sustain activity (Lorente de No, 1938).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorente de No, 1938

claim: Hebb's idea of cell assemblies suggested that ensembles of cells encoded a particular neuronal concept.
source: Hebb's idea of cell assemblies suggested that ensembles of cells encoded a particular neuronal concept, but also that there was sequential activation within the group of cells forming the assembly (Hebb, 1949).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hebb, 1949

claim: There was sequential activation within the group of cells forming the assembly in Hebb's cell assemblies.
source: Hebb's idea of cell assemblies suggested that ensembles of cells encoded a particular neuronal concept, but also that there was sequential activation within the group of cells forming the assembly (Hebb, 1949).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hebb, 1949

claim: Many sensory systems process sequential stimuli that are typically mapped to ensembles of sequentially active neurons.
source: Many sensory systems process sequential stimuli, and these are typically mapped to ensembles of sequentially active neurons (Bouchard and Brainard, 2016; Broome et al., 2006; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouchard and Brainard, 2016; Broome et al., 2006; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015

claim: Hippocampal place cells represent a higher-order cognitive map of space.
source: Deeper in the brain, hippocampal place cells represent a higher-order cognitive map of space, yet here too sequences occur when the animal moves through spatial locations represented by the place cells (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson and McNaughton, 1994

claim: Sequences occur in hippocampal place cells when the animal moves through spatial locations represented by the place cells.
source: Deeper in the brain, hippocampal place cells represent a higher-order cognitive map of space, yet here too sequences occur when the animal moves through spatial locations represented by the place cells (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson and McNaughton, 1994

claim: The hippocampus exhibits sequential activity in the form of fast replay events.
source: The hippocampus exhibits other forms of sequential activity in the form of fast replay events (Jadhav et al., 2012; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and stimulus-bridging activity that emerges during associative learning (MacDonald et al., 2011) and trace conditioning (Modi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jadhav et al., 2012; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994

claim: The hippocampus exhibits stimulus-bridging activity that emerges during associative learning.
source: The hippocampus exhibits other forms of sequential activity in the form of fast replay events (Jadhav et al., 2012; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and stimulus-bridging activity that emerges during associative learning (MacDonald et al., 2011) and trace conditioning (Modi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2011

claim: The hippocampus exhibits stimulus-bridging activity that emerges during trace conditioning.
source: The hippocampus exhibits other forms of sequential activity in the form of fast replay events (Jadhav et al., 2012; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and stimulus-bridging activity that emerges during associative learning (MacDonald et al., 2011) and trace conditioning (Modi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Modi et al., 2014

claim: The idea of synfire chains examines conditions for self-sustaining sequential activity to occur in multiple layers of a network.
source: The idea of synfire chains examines conditions for self-sustaining sequential activity to occur in multiple layers of a network (Abeles, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abeles, 1982

claim: Excessive activation in synfire chains can lead to runaway epileptiform activity.
source: This is non-trivial, as excessive activation can lead to runaway epileptiform activity, whereas insufficient activation causes decay of the activity wave (Kumar et al., 2008; Mehring et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2008; Mehring et al., 2003

claim: Insufficient activation in synfire chains causes decay of the activity wave.
source: This is non-trivial, as excessive activation can lead to runaway epileptiform activity, whereas insufficient activation causes decay of the activity wave (Kumar et al., 2008; Mehring et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2008; Mehring et al., 2003

claim: Events may be run through a delay line so that the oldest event is delayed more, allowing classical attractor networks to recognize patterns in the sequence.
source: For example, events may be run through a delay line, so that the oldest event is delayed more, the next event less, and so on, so that they all arrive at the neural network at the same time. Thus, the time-sequence is flattened in time and classical attractor networks can recognize patterns in the sequence (Tank and Hopfield, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tank and Hopfield, 1987

claim: Time-varying attractor networks have been shown to be able to implement and recognize sequences.
source: Time-varying attractor networks have also been shown to be able to implement and recognize sequences (Lee, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee, 2002

claim: Recursive networks using supervised learning and short-term synaptic plasticity have been shown to implement time-invariance.
source: Recursive networks using supervised learning, and short-term synaptic plasticity have been shown to be implement time-invariance (Barak and Tsodyks, 2006; Goudar and Buonomano, 2015; Laje and Buonomano, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barak and Tsodyks, 2006; Goudar and Buonomano, 2015; Laje and Buonomano, 2013

claim: The theory of Hierarchical Temporal Memory builds on the idea of sequence-recognizing neurons and networks as a way to perform complex temporal computation.
source: The theory of Hierarchical Temporal Memory builds on the idea of sequence-recognizing neurons and networks as a way to perform complex temporal computation (George and Hawkins, 2009; Hawkins and Ahmad, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to George and Hawkins, 2009; Hawkins and Ahmad, 2016

claim: Rall showed theoretically that synaptic events propagate down the dendritic tree with a small delay.
source: One of the first biophysical proposals for subcellular sequence recognition was made by Rall, who showed theoretically that synaptic events propagate down the dendritic tree with a small delay. By timing synaptic inputs to coincide with this delay, Rall predicted that ordered input should yield a larger response than reversed input (Rall, 1964).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rall, 1964

claim: Rall predicted that ordered input should yield a larger response than reversed input when synaptic inputs are timed to coincide with the delay of synaptic event propagation.
source: One of the first biophysical proposals for subcellular sequence recognition was made by Rall, who showed theoretically that synaptic events propagate down the dendritic tree with a small delay. By timing synaptic inputs to coincide with this delay, Rall predicted that ordered input should yield a larger response than reversed input (Rall, 1964).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rall, 1964

claim: Branco et al. experimentally demonstrated that NMDA receptor amplification of 'inward' sequences (distal to proximal) gave rise to about 40% larger somatic depolarization than 'outward' sequences for rapid (~40 ms) sequences.
source: A stronger version of this mechanism was experimentally demonstrated by Branco et al. (2010) who used glutamate uncaging to provide sequential input along a pyramidal neuron dendrite. They showed that NMDA receptor amplification of 'inward' sequences (distal to proximal) gave rise to about 40% larger somatic depolarization than 'outward' sequences, for rapid (~40 ms) sequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to Branco et al. (2010)

claim: Synaptically-driven reaction-diffusion pathways on dendrites can perform sequence discrimination on behaviorally relevant time-scales.
source: Here, we show that synaptically-driven reaction-diffusion pathways on dendrites can perform sequence discrimination on behaviorally relevant time-scales.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the modeling data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: Selectivity in abstract signaling models arises when inputs at successive locations are aligned with and amplified by propagating chemical waves triggered by previous inputs.
source: We used abstract signaling models to show that selectivity arises when inputs at successive locations are aligned with, and amplified by, propagating chemical waves triggered by previous inputs.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figures 2-4

claim: Sequential synaptic input onto spines in morphologically, electrically, and chemically detailed pyramidal neuronal models based on rat data can recognize sequences.
source: We incorporated biological detail using sequential synaptic input onto spines in morphologically, electrically, and chemically detailed pyramidal neuronal models based on rat data. Again, sequences were recognized, and local channel modulation downstream of putative sequence-triggered signaling could elicit changes in neuronal firing.
evidence: Supported by the detailed modeling results shown in Figures 5-7

claim: Local channel modulation downstream of putative sequence-triggered signaling could elicit changes in neuronal firing.
source: We incorporated biological detail using sequential synaptic input onto spines in morphologically, electrically, and chemically detailed pyramidal neuronal models based on rat data. Again, sequences were recognized, and local channel modulation downstream of putative sequence-triggered signaling could elicit changes in neuronal firing.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: Dendritic sequence-recognition zones occupy 5 to 30 microns.
source: We predict that dendritic sequence-recognition zones occupy 5 to 30 microns and recognize time-intervals of 0.2 to 5 s.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6

claim: Dendritic sequence-recognition zones recognize time-intervals of 0.2 to 5 s.
source: We predict that dendritic sequence-recognition zones occupy 5 to 30 microns and recognize time-intervals of 0.2 to 5 s.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6

claim: The feedback inhibition model showed no input sequence-dependent difference in total activity.
source: First, we found that the simple feedback inhibition model showed no input sequence-dependent difference in total activity.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2, first column

claim: The feedforward inhibition model showed a small amount of selectivity.
source: Then, we observed that the feedforward inhibition model showed a small amount of selectivity (Figure 2D–G).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D-G, second column

claim: The FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) model was strongly selective, with a large buildup of response only when the input was sequential.
source: The FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) model was strongly selective, with a large buildup of response only when the input was sequential (Figure 2 third column, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2, third column, and Video 3

claim: The switching model was the most selective.
source: The switching model was the most selective (Figure 2 last column, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2, last column, and Video 4

claim: Strong selectivity emerged from a supralinear buildup of responses when diffusively propagating activity was aligned with successive inputs.
source: Thus, this set of simulations showed that several reaction-diffusion like systems were capable of sequence selectivity. Strong selectivity emerged from a supralinear buildup of responses when diffusively propagating activity was aligned with successive inputs, and suppression due to inhibition when the alignment was off.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 2

claim: Suppression due to inhibition occurs when the alignment of diffusively propagating activity with successive inputs is off.
source: Thus, this set of simulations showed that several reaction-diffusion like systems were capable of sequence selectivity. Strong selectivity emerged from a supralinear buildup of responses when diffusively propagating activity was aligned with successive inputs, and suppression due to inhibition when the alignment was off.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 2

claim: Scaling all rates and diffusion constants by the same factor scaled the sequence speed to which the network had the strongest response.
source: We first tested the most straightforward assumption, that sequence propagation speed was proportional to chemical rate and diffusion constants. To do this, we scaled all rates and the diffusion constants by the same factor, and reduced the stimulus width by the same factor. We ran the same grid of stimulus space and time intervals as above. As expected, scaling all the chemical and diffusion rates also scaled the sequence speed to which the network had the strongest response.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4A-E

claim: As the rates were increased, the best tuning was at shorter time intervals but roughly the same spatial intervals.
source: As the rates were increased, the best tuning was at shorter time intervals but roughly the same spatial intervals. (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4A-E

claim: The tuning zone depended on stimulus strength.
source: We therefore also examined dependence of tuning on stimulus strength, and observed that the tuning zone also depended on stimulus strength (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4F,G

claim: Selectivity was robust to some parameters, such as diffusion constants, but fragile (range ~20%) with respect to some rate constants and stimulus amplitude.
source: We found that selectivity was robust to some parameters, such as diffusion constants, but fragile (range ~20%) with respect to some rate constants and stimulus amplitude.
evidence: Supported by the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: By varying rates for reactions and diffusion, good sequence selectivity was achieved over a broad range of time-intervals (0.5–4 s between stimuli) and spatial intervals (2–6 μm between stimuli).
source: Thus, by varying rates for reactions and diffusion, we were able to achieve good sequence selectivity over a broad range of time-intervals (0.5–4 s between stimuli) and spatial intervals (2–6 μm between stimuli).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: A mass-action reaction-diffusion system based on MAPK feedback and bistability exhibited sequence selectivity when it had switch-like turnon with delayed turnoff by negative feedback.
source: Thus, we showed that a mass-action reaction-diffusion system exhibited sequence selectivity when it had switch-like turnon with delayed turnoff by negative feedback.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5

claim: The model neuron exhibited theta-modulated sub-threshold oscillations with spiking activity at ~1 Hz due to background synaptic input.
source: Due to the background synaptic input, the model exhibited theta-modulated sub-threshold oscillations, with spiking activity at ~1 Hz (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6B

claim: Strong selectivity in MAPK activity for sequential stimuli as compared to scrambled was observed in the basal dendrite.
source: With these parameters, we observed strong selectivity in MAPK activity for sequential stimuli as compared to scrambled in the basal dendrite (Figure 6D, solid lines for sequential vs. dashed for scrambled).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6D

claim: Strong sequence selectivity was observed in the basal dendrite zone for a restricted range of space and time intervals.
source: We observed strong sequence selectivity in the basal dendrite zone, for a restricted range of space and time intervals, as expected from the earlier calculations (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6E-G

claim: There were strongly sequence selective responses in oblique dendrites and distal apical dendritic regions, but these required stronger stimuli.
source: We found that there were indeed strongly sequence selective responses in oblique dendrites and distal apical dendritic regions, but these required stronger stimuli (Figure 6H,I; Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6H,I and Videos 6 and 7

claim: Sequence recognition was not observed in the primary apical dendrite.
source: We did not observe sequence recognition in the primary apical dendrite (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6J

claim: The model retained selectivity (at least 50% of best selectivity) over a factor of ~2 or more for all parameters except the Raf affinity for Ca2+.
source: Even though we had not fine-tuned the model for robustness, we found that the model retained selectivity (at least 50% of best selectivity) over a factor of ~2 or more for all parameters except the Raf affinity for Ca2+ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The Raf affinity for Ca2+ parameter could be varied by ±15% about its reference.
source: The latter parameter could be varied by ±15% about its reference.
evidence: Supported by the parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Intracellular signaling pathways exhibited selectivity for ordered synaptic input, even when considerable morphological and electrical detail and noisy input were incorporated.
source: Thus, we showed that intracellular signaling pathways exhibited selectivity for ordered synaptic input, even when considerable morphological and electrical detail and noisy input were incorporated.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results shown in Figure 6

claim: Modulation of the Na channel in the apical and primary dendrites could increase firing rates by large factors.
source: We found that modulation of the Na channel, and increase in nonselective leak conductance in the apical and primary dendrites could increase firing rates by large factors (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: Increase in nonselective leak conductance in the apical and primary dendrites could increase firing rates by large factors.
source: We found that modulation of the Na channel, and increase in nonselective leak conductance in the apical and primary dendrites could increase firing rates by large factors (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: A 10x increase in AMPAR conductance in the 20 μm zone in the apical dendrite led to a doubling in cell firing.
source: With this change, we found that a 10x increase in AMPAR conductance in the 20 μm zone in the apical dendrite led to a doubling in cell firing (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7C

claim: A similar manipulation in the primary dendrite led to a shallower increase in cell firing, about 1.5x.
source: A similar manipulation in the primary dendrite led to a shallower increase, about 1.5x.
evidence: Supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7C

claim: Chemical signaling in rather small regions of the apical dendrite may lead to a rapid change in cell firing by local channel modulation.
source: Thus, chemical signaling, even in rather small regions of the apical dendrite, may lead to a rapid change in cell firing by local channel modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results shown in Figure 7

claim: Large channel modulations were needed to elicit sufficiently large (e.g., 50%) changes in firing rate that could be detected over the noisy background.
source: However, large channel modulations were needed to elicit sufficiently large (e.g., 50%) changes in in firing rate that could be detected over the noisy background.

source: For example, MAPK phosphorylates and modulates KA (Yuan et al., 2002) Kir6.2 (Lin and Chai, 2008), and Na(v) 1.7channels (Stamboulian et al., 2010).

claim: MAPK phosphorylates and modulates Na(v) 1.7 channels.

source: Similar brief, strong synaptic input on small sections of distal dendrites has been reported to cause strong changes in activity of striatal spiny neurons by triggering a transition to an 'up' state (Plotkin et al., 2011).

source: Another might be local CICR, which has already been proposed to support propagating wave activity in dendrites (Hagenston et al., 2008; Kapur et al., 2001; Larkum et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2016; Plotkin et al., 2013; Ross, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagenston et al., 2008; Kapur et al., 2001; Larkum et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2016; Plotkin et al., 2013; Ross, 2012

claim: CICR has faster dynamics, of the order of 100 μm/s.
source: These have faster dynamics, of the order of 100 μm/s.

claim: The length-scale of dendritic CICR is similar (~10–20 μm) to that envisaged for sequence recognition in this study.
source: Further, dendritic Ca2+ imaging suggests that the length-scale of dendritic CICR is similar (~10–20 μm) to that envisaged for sequence recognition in our study (Hagenston et al., 2008; Kapur et al., 2001; Larkum et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagenston et al., 2008; Kapur et al., 2001; Larkum et al., 2003

source: Still faster sequence recognition (~40 ms) has been demonstrated in the electrical domain, where forward sequences can be discriminated from backward (Branco et al., 2010).

claim: Electrical sequence recognition has been shown to have ~40% discrimination between forward and backward patterns.
source: This electrical mechanism has been shown to have ~40% discrimination between forward and backward patterns, rather than the strong selectivity among permutations of patterns shown by our chemical system.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with the cited work of Branco et al., 2010

claim: All modeling was carried out using MOOSE, the Multiscale Object-Oriented Simulation Environment.
source: All modeling was carried out using MOOSE, the Multiscale Object-Oriented Simulation Environment (Ray and Bhalla, 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Ray and Bhalla, 2008

claim: MOOSE utilizes the GNU Scientific Library (GSL) Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg fifth order method for chemical computations.
source: MOOSE utilizes the GNU Scientific Library (GSL) Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg fifth order method for chemical computations, and a custom-written branching 1-D diffusion solver using the backward Euler (implicit) method.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the software used

claim: Stochastic chemical calculations were carried out using a custom-written optimized version of the Gillespie Stochastic Systems Algorithm.
source: Stochastic chemical calculations were carried out using a custom-written optimized version of the Gillespie Stochastic Systems Algorithm.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the computational methods used

claim: Electrical computations utilized a custom version of the branched nerve equation solution methods described by Hines.
source: Electrical computations utilized a custom version of the branched nerve equation solution methods described by Hines (Hines, 1984).

claim: The electrical computation method has been validated by comparison with other simulators.
source: This has been validated by comparison with other simulators (Gleeson et al., 2010).

claim: Electrical model morphologies were either geometrical (cylindrical) or derived from published cell reconstructions available on NeuroMorpho.org.

evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to Ascoli et al., 2007; Dougherty et al., 2012

claim: Spines were positioned along dendrites using Poisson statistics with a specified mean spacing between spines (1 μm in the full cell model).
source: Spines were positioned along dendrites using Poisson statistics with a specified mean spacing between spines (1 μm in the full cell model).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the model construction

claim: Spines were modeled as a cylindrical head (0.5 μm length and diameter) on a cylindrical shaft (1 μm length, 0.2 μm diameter).
source: Spines were modeled as a cylindrical head (0.5 μm length and diameter) on a cylindrical shaft (1 μm length, 0.2 μm diameter).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the model construction

claim: Channel kinetics were derived from Traub et al. (1991).
source: Channel kinetics were derived from Traub et al. (1991).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Traub et al. (1991)

claim: Abstract reaction-diffusion calculations were carried out in a 1-dimensional geometry with spatial discretization of 1 μm.
source: Abstract reaction-diffusion calculations (Figures 2–4) were carried out in a 1-dimensional geometry with spatial discretization of 1 μm.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the model construction

claim: The reaction systems were active only in five equally spaced 1 μm patches, but diffusion took place throughout the 100 μm length of the model.
source: In order to represent reactions occurring in a spatially restricted region in or under dendritic spines, the reaction systems were active only in five equally spaced 1 μm patches, but diffusion took place throughout the 100 μm length of the model.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the model construction

claim: Recursive sequence recognition is a fundamental computational operation in the brain.
source: We postulate that recursive sequence recognition is a fundamental computational operation in the brain, and that this operation may be implemented by neurons able to recognize spatially and temporally sequential input on behavioral time-scales (seconds).
evidence: This is a postulate/hypothesis of the study

claim: This mechanism provides highly parallel and selective neural computation in a functionally important time range.
source: We suggest that this mechanism provides highly parallel and selective neural computation in a functionally important time range.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the modeling results throughout the manuscript

claim: There are at least four major kinases (PKA, PKC, MAPK, CaMKII) that may fit the profile of state switching with feedback inhibition.
source: There are several synaptically activated pathways that may fit the profile of state switching with feedback inhibition. Based on our abstract models (Figure 2), these are candidates for implementing sequence selectivity. These include four major kinases (PKA, PKC, MAPK, CaMKII) and a variety of second-messenger and metabotropic pathways (Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999; Kim et al., 2011; Lisman and Zhabotinsky, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999; Kim et al., 2011; Lisman and Zhabotinsky, 2001

claim: If a 5-stage sequence is considered, a perfect sequence recognizer would distinguish 1 from 5! possible sequences, or 1 in 120.
source: If we take a 5-stage sequence, a perfect sequence recognizer would distinguish 1 from 5! possible sequences, or 1 in 120.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on combinatorics

claim: In a pyramidal neuron with about 10000 μm of dendritic length, there are ~1000 non-overlapping sequence recognition blocks of 10 μm each.
source: Say the set of spines occupies 10 μm. The most conservative calculation requires that these blocks do not overlap, so in a pyramidal neuron with about 10000 μm of dendritic length we have ~1000 blocks.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the modeling results and known neuronal anatomy

claim: If blocks are permitted to slide by one input at a time, there are five times as many sequence recognition blocks, i.e., ~5000.
source: If we permit blocks to slide by one input at a time, there are five times as many sequence recognition blocks, i.e., ~5000.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the modeling results

claim: The neuron may perform 500 sequence discriminations each second.
source: If the sequence lasts 10 s, a single block performs 0.1 sequence recognitions per second. Thus, the neuron may perform 500 sequence discriminations each second.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the modeling results

claim: Each neuron has ~5000 blocks and can recognize ~8.5×10^7 sequences.
source: Using our calculation above, each neuron has ~5000 blocks, and so can recognize ~8.5×107 sequences.
evidence: This is a speculative calculation based on assumptions about connectivity and sparsity

claim: The hypothesis of single-cell sequence recognition is readily testable using current technology.
source: Our hypothesis of single-cell sequence recognition is readily testable using current technology.
evidence: This is a statement about the testability of the hypothesis

claim: The chemical basis of sequence recognition may be examined in brain-slice using local agonist application or sequential glutamate uncaging followed by microscopic readouts of activity reporters for candidate pathways.
source: Its chemical basis may be examined in brain-slice using local agonist application or sequential glutamate uncaging followed by microscopic readouts of activity reporters for candidate pathways.
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental testing

claim: Experiments have shown that there is a buildup of Ca2+ along small, 20 μm stretches of dendrite under suitable stimulus conditions.
source: Such experiments have already been done to examine CICR triggered by synaptic inputs converging to adjacent synapses (Hagenston et al., 2008; Plotkin et al., 2013). These show that there is indeed a buildup of Ca2+ along small, 20 μm stretches of dendrite, under suitable stimulus conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagenston et al., 2008; Plotkin et al., 2013
